Designing a Distributed Cache: From a Simple In-Memory Store to a Scalable, Fault-Tolerant System
Modern systems live and die by latency. Databases are powerful, but they’re rarely fast enough to serve every request directly - especially at scale. That’s where distributed caches come in.
In this article, we’ll walk through the end-to-end design of a distributed cache, starting from a single-node in-memory store and evolving it into a highly available, scalable, and fault-tolerant system capable of handling 100,000 requests per second and up to 1 TB of cached data.
This mirrors the kind of design decisions used in real-world systems similar to Redis, Memcached, and large-scale internal caches at major tech companies.
What Are We Building?
At its core, the system is a key–value cache. While the concept is simple, requirements around performance, availability, and scale quickly turn it into a distributed systems problem.
Before diving into architecture, let’s define what the cache must do.
Functional Requirements
The cache must behave predictably while remaining fast and easy to scale.
Basic Cache Operations
The system supports:
•
Get: Retrieve a value by key
•
Set: Insert or update a key–value pair
•
Delete: Explicitly remove a key
These operations must remain efficient under heavy concurrent access.
Time-Based Expiration (TTL)
Each key can optionally have a time-to-live (TTL):
•
Once expired, the key becomes invalid
•
Expired entries should never be returned
TTL prevents stale data from occupying memory indefinitely.
Capacity-Based Eviction (LRU)
Since memory is limited, the cache uses a Least Recently Used (LRU) eviction strategy:
•
Frequently accessed items stay in memory
•
Cold data is evicted first
This ensures optimal use of available RAM.
Expected System Scale
The cache is designed for high traffic and large datasets.
•
Total data size: Up to 1 TB
•
Throughput: Approximately 100,000 requests per second
•
Access pattern: Predominantly read-heavy (~90% reads)
These constraints rule out a single-node solution and require horizontal scaling.
Non-Functional Requirements
Because this is a cache and not a source of truth, priorities differ from traditional databases.
High Availability
The system must continue serving traffic even if some nodes fail.
Availability Over Strong Consistency
Serving slightly stale data is acceptable if it improves uptime and latency.
Low-Latency Reads
•
Target P95 latency under 10 ms
High Throughput
The cache must not become a bottleneck for downstream services.
Core Data Model
The cache revolves around a small set of core concepts.
Record (Key–Value Pair)
A unique key mapped to an associated value.
Expiration (TTL)
An optional expiration timestamp that determines when a key is invalidated.
Public API Design
The cache exposes a simple HTTP-based API.
Insert or Update a Key
POST /cache
{ "key": "string", "value": "json", "ttl": "seconds" }
Inserts or updates a key with an optional TTL.
Retrieve a Key
GET /cache/{key}
{ "value": "json", "ttl": "seconds_remaining" }
Returns the value if the key exists and has not expired.
Delete a Key
DELETE /cache/{key} Explicitly removes the key from the cache.
Starting Simple: Single-Node Cache Design
The system begins as a single-node in-memory cache.
•
Clients communicate directly with the cache service
•
Data is stored in an in-memory hash map
•
Persistence is not required
To support concurrent access, the cache uses thread-safe data structures or fine-grained locking.
This design offers extremely fast reads and writes and serves as the foundation for scaling.
Implementing TTL (Time-To-Live)
Each cache entry includes an expiration timestamp.
Lazy Expiration
On each request:
•
The current time is compared with the TTL
•
Expired keys are immediately deleted
This approach minimizes overhead for frequently accessed keys.
The Need for Background Cleanup
Keys that expire but are never accessed again would otherwise remain in memory.
To address this:
•
A background cleanup job periodically scans the cache
•
Expired entries are removed to reclaim memory
LRU Eviction Strategy
To implement LRU efficiently, the cache uses:
•
A hash map for O(1) lookups
•
A doubly linked list to track access order
How It Works
•
Accessed or inserted keys move to the head
•
When capacity is reached, keys at the tail are evicted
All operations complete in constant time.
Scaling to Multiple Nodes
A single node cannot handle the required scale.
Sharding with Consistent Hashing
•
Keys are distributed across nodes deterministically
•
Adding or removing nodes remaps only a small portion of keys
•
Enables smooth horizontal scaling
From this point forward, the cache operates as a cluster.
High Availability and Fault Tolerance
Performance alone is not enough - resilience is essential.
Asynchronous Primary–Replica Replication
Each shard consists of:
•
One primary node (handles writes)
•
One or more replica nodes
Writes are acknowledged immediately by the primary and replicated asynchronously, resulting in:
•
Low write latency
•
High availability
•
Eventual consistency
Failure Detection and Leader Election
Nodes send regular heartbeats to a coordination service such as etcd, ZooKeeper, or a Raft-based system.
If a primary fails:
•
Its leadership lease expires
•
A replica is promoted to primary
•
The coordination service ensures a single leader
This prevents split-brain scenarios.
Handling Failover
During failover:
•
Writes may pause briefly
•
Reads can continue from replicas
•
Some requests may temporarily fall back to the database
Because the cache is not the source of truth, these tradeoffs are acceptable.
Scaling the Cache to 1 TB
Memory capacity is the primary scaling constraint.
For example:
•
A 32 GB RAM node can safely allocate ~24 GB for cache data
Reaching 1 TB requires:
•
Adding more nodes
•
Redistributing keys via consistent hashing
As storage scales, throughput naturally increases as well.
Final Thoughts
Designing a distributed cache is a step-by-step evolution:
•
Start with a fast in-memory store
•
Add TTL and eviction policies
•
Distribute data across nodes
•
Replicate for availability
•
Coordinate for fault tolerance
The end result is a cache that is fast, scalable, and resilient, capable of supporting modern, high-traffic applications with minimal latency.
If you’re preparing for system design interviews or building real-world infrastructure, understanding this progression is invaluable.
